subject: Clarify packaging: token consolidation, minimums, and crediting approach
messages:
From: Timothy Lowe <tim@acmehealth.com>
To: olga_petrov <olga@redwood.example>
Cc: contracts@acmehealth.com
Date: 2026-02-25T09:14:00-08:00
Subject: Clarify token rounding & minimums for pilot

Olga — thanks again for the demo yesterday. Two quick items the procurement team asked us to clarify before we move to procurement: 

1) How you round token usage for streaming calls versus discrete requests (per-call vs per-session). Do you round up to the next whole token, or do you aggregate within a billing window?
2) If we hit a short burst below the minimum (we expect lots of sub-100-token calls during triage flows), do those get credited against the monthly minimum or billed separately?

If you can send a short worked example (PDF or spreadsheet) showing an hour of mixed traffic and how it maps to invoice lines, that would be ideal. Also cc'd contracts for SOW alignment.

—Tim
Director of AI, Acme Health

Subject: Re: Clarify token rounding & minimums for pilot

Tim — thanks, good questions. High-level TL;DR up front:

- We aggregate usage into a rolling 1-hour billing window for context-smoothing (default for hosted API pilots).
- Within that window we compute token consumption per request and sum; we then apply the per-unit quantum (100-token quantum in your draft proposal) and round up to the nearest quantum for invoice line items.
- Short bursts below minimums are first applied to any monthly committed units (if you have a commitment). For pure pay-as-you-go pilots with a monthly minimum, we credit short-burst usage against the minimum so you don’t see double-charging.

I attached a worked spreadsheet (redwood_pricing_exhibit_v2.xlsx) showing an hour of mixed traffic, comparing: per-call rounding vs rolling-window aggregation vs commit-applied crediting. Note the summary tab has the final invoice mapping.

Next steps: Kimberly will propose two packaging options (pilot PAYG with smoothing credits, or a small committed pool with an overage quantum). Kim — can you put numbers and a short example for Acme? Rafael, FYI on the KV-cache note below.

Thanks,
Olga Petrov

Subject: Re: Clarify token rounding & minimums for pilot — packaging options + math

Tim — quick packaging options, with conservative math based on the spreadsheet: 

Option A — PAYG smoothing credits (no commit)
- Quantum: 100 tokens
- Billing window: rolling 1-hour aggregation
- Rounding: aggregate tokens in window then round up to nearest 100
- Example (from sheet): 2,340 total tokens in hour -> round to 2,400 -> invoiced units = 24 quanta
- Pilot concession: we apply a \"smoothing credit\" equal to 1 quantum per 200 quanta used for the first 3 months (helps microburst-heavy customers)

Option B — Small committed pool (3k tokens/day equivalent)
- Monthly commitment converts to committed quanta first; overage billed at quantum rate with no smoothing credit
- Example: month has 10 days of heavy triage plus 20 low-activity days — commit absorbs 80% of heavy bursts; overage is predictable and often cheaper per-quanta

Practical recommendation: for your traffic profile (many short sub-100 calls but predictable daily volume), Option B with a 30% smoothing buffer in the first 60 days yields the lowest bill volatility.

I'll attach a one-page summary for procurement and a redlined pricing exhibit for SOW.

Subject: Re: Clarify token rounding & minimums for pilot — technical caveats

Quick technical notes to make the invoice mapping accurate:

- KV cache reuse: when you have repeated prompts within the same session, internal token emission is lower. Our metering counts output + consumed context tokens at the request boundary; when we aggregate in the 1-hour window we include cache hits as reduced consumption. The example spreadsheet already includes a 12% KV reuse assumption; we can adjust that to your measured telemetry if you provide sample logs.

- Streaming vs finalization: streaming frames are tallied as they finalize into the response. There is no double-charge for partial frames — only final token counts are aggregated.

- Long context anchoring: if you pin long context across requests (e.g., a 16k anchor for each call), that context is counted per call unless you use our session affinity and context-siloing, which reduces repeated context counts. If you want, we can enable a session-keyed cache for the pilot to limit anchor recharges.

I'll help annotate the pricing exhibit with these assumptions.

—Rafael
